note: Read-first briefs, one per syllabus section. Rebuilt 2026-10-27 to match SAFe study app format: PURPOSE openers, exam traps, real-world scenarios, HTML formatting. ITIL 4 Foundation content verified against AXELOS sample papers and candidate syllabus.

concepts.lead: This section is pure vocabulary — 5 marks that come down to knowing ITIL's narrow, specific definitions. The exam gives you a scenario and asks you to name the concept, not explain it. The trap is that ITIL defines words you already use (value, service, risk) but defines them MORE NARROWLY than everyday English. Every question hinges on one or two keywords baked into the official definition. Know those keywords cold and these 5 marks are yours.
list: Value — and the keyword 'perceived' that decides the exam question
Service — co-creation, outcomes, and who absorbs costs and risks
Service offering — the packaged bundle (goods, access, service actions)
Output vs outcome — the distinction the exam tests hardest in this section
Cost and risk — why both flow in BOTH directions
Utility and warranty — fitness for purpose vs fitness for use (most reversed pair)
The three consumer roles — customer, user, sponsor (one person or three)
Service management — the keyword is 'specialized organizational capabilities'
Organization and risk — even one person counts as an organization
Service provision, consumption, and relationship management — how provider and consumer connect

items.name: Value
items.body:
PURPOSE: everything in ITIL 4 starts here. Value is the reason services exist, the reason practices exist, and the foundation of the first guiding principle. Without a clear definition of value, the rest of the framework has no anchor.

Definition: the perceived benefits, usefulness, and importance of something.

'Perceived' is the exam keyword. Value is not what the provider delivers — it is what the stakeholder EXPERIENCES. Two consumers can get identical service and perceive completely different value. The provider does not get to declare value; the consumer judges it.

In your release management world, this is the difference between a release that shipped every planned feature on time and a release that actually moved the metric the business cared about. You have seen portal teams hit every sprint goal while the business still said 'this is not what we needed.' Outputs delivered, value missed.

EXAM TRAP: any answer that says value is defined by the provider, or measured only by the provider's metrics, is wrong. Value is always co-created and always judged by the stakeholder.

items.name: Service
items.body:
PURPOSE: this definition is the backbone of the entire framework. Every other concept — practices, the value chain, dimensions — exists to support service delivery. Understanding the definition tells you what ITIL cares about.

Definition: a means of enabling value co-creation by facilitating outcomes customers want, without the customer having to manage specific costs and risks.

Three things are built into that single sentence:
1. Co-creation — the provider cannot deliver value alone. The consumer must participate.
2. Outcomes — the service exists for results, not activities.
3. Cost and risk absorption — the provider takes on costs and risks so the consumer does not have to.

In your release management world, your scrum teams did not manage the deployment infrastructure, the change schedule, or the production risk. You absorbed that for them — that is service in ITIL terms.

EXAM TRAP: any answer describing a service that mentions only outputs (deliverables) instead of outcomes (results for stakeholders) is the distractor. Any answer claiming the provider delivers value unilaterally misses 'co-creation.'

items.name: Service offering
items.body:
PURPOSE: a service offering is how the provider packages a service for a specific consumer group. It turns the abstract concept of 'service' into something a consumer can actually choose and consume.

Definition: a formal description of one or more services, designed for a specific target consumer group.

An offering bundles three things:
1. Goods — things transferred to the consumer (a laptop, a license)
2. Access to resources — things the consumer can use but does not own (a network, a platform)
3. Service actions — things done for the consumer (user support, monitoring)

The distinction from 'service': the service is the underlying capability. The offering is the packaged, named thing a consumer picks from — like a menu item versus the kitchen that prepares it.

EXAM TRAP: the exam may describe a bundle of goods, access, and actions, then ask what it is. The answer is 'service offering,' not 'service.' If the question emphasizes what is being made available to a specific consumer group, it is pointing at the offering.

items.name: Output vs outcome
items.body:
PURPOSE: this distinction is probably the most heavily tested concept in this section. It forces you to separate what you PRODUCED from what HAPPENED because of it.

Output: a tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity.
Outcome: a result for a stakeholder, enabled by one or more outputs.

In your release management world, this is the release that shipped every planned feature on schedule — outputs delivered — but moved nothing for the business because the features did not match what users actually needed. Every output was checked off. The outcome was missed.

The reverse also happens: a single hotfix that restored a broken checkout flow (one small output) produced a massive business outcome because revenue recovered immediately.

EXAM TRAP: the exam will describe a scenario where all deliverables were completed but the business result was not achieved, then ask you to name the gap. The answer is outcome. If it describes what was produced, that is the output. If it describes what changed for the stakeholder, that is the outcome.

items.name: Cost and risk — both directions
items.body:
PURPOSE: services are not free gifts. They remove some costs and risks from the consumer AND impose others. Understanding this two-way flow is essential to understanding value.

Costs removed from the consumer: infrastructure, staffing, operational effort — the consumer does not have to build and run the capability themselves.
Costs imposed on the consumer: subscription fees, adoption effort, training, integration work.

Risks removed from the consumer: the provider handles availability, security, and operational continuity.
Risks imposed on the consumer: vendor lock-in, dependency on the provider's reliability, loss of direct control.

In your release management world, when a scrum team moved their content deployment to LaunchDarkly, they removed the risk of a bad deploy affecting all users at once. But they picked up a new risk: dependency on LaunchDarkly's availability.

EXAM TRAP: any answer claiming the cost or risk flow only goes one direction is wrong. Services ALWAYS remove some and impose others. The exam tests whether you understand both sides.

items.name: Utility and warranty
items.body:
PURPOSE: these two concepts together define whether a service is fit to create value. Both are required — one without the other is incomplete.

Utility = fitness for purpose — what the service DOES. Does it meet the need?
Warranty = fitness for use — how WELL it performs. Is it available, fast enough, secure, and resilient?

A service with perfect uptime that does the wrong thing has warranty but no utility. A service that does exactly the right thing but goes down every Tuesday has utility but no warranty. Both must be present for value.

Warranty covers four areas: availability, capacity, security, and continuity. Think of it as the non-functional requirements — the service works, and it works well enough, often enough, safely enough, and reliably enough.

In your release management world, a deployment pipeline that ran perfectly but deployed to the wrong environment would have warranty (it performed reliably) but no utility (it did the wrong thing).

EXAM TRAP: reversing utility and warranty is the single most common miss in this section. Mnemonic: utility = purpose (what it does), warranty = how well (performance).

items.name: The three consumer roles
items.body:
PURPOSE: ITIL splits the consumer side into three roles because the person who pays, the person who uses, and the person who defines requirements may have completely different views of value. The framework needs to address all three.

Customer: defines requirements and takes responsibility for outcomes of service consumption.
User: the person who actually uses the service day to day.
Sponsor: authorizes the budget for service consumption.

One person can hold all three roles, or they can be three different people with conflicting priorities. A sponsor may approve a cheaper tool; the users may hate it; the customer may not have been consulted at all.

In your release management world, your customer was the scrum team lead defining what needed to ship. Your users were the developers and testers consuming the release process. Your sponsor was the director who funded the tooling and headcount.

EXAM TRAP: questions use the specific role name to signal which perspective matters. If the question says 'customer,' it is asking about requirements and outcomes. If it says 'user,' it is asking about day-to-day experience. If it says 'sponsor,' it is asking about budget authorization. Do not treat them as interchangeable.

items.name: Service management
items.body:
PURPOSE: this term describes what organizations must BUILD INTERNALLY to deliver services — it is not a framework, a process, or a tool.

Definition: a set of specialized organizational capabilities for enabling value to customers in the form of services.

The keyword is 'specialized organizational capabilities.' It describes what the organization CAN DO, not what methodology it follows. An organization with mature service management has people, processes, technology, and information organized specifically for creating value through services.

In your release management world, you built a specialized capability at Cigna — intake automation, deployment gates, the war room escalation framework, the release health dashboard. That entire system of people, tools, and processes was service management applied to the release function.

EXAM TRAP: if an answer defines service management as a framework, a set of tools, or a methodology, it is wrong. It is about organizational capabilities — what the organization is structured and equipped to do.

items.name: Organization and risk
items.body:
PURPOSE: ITIL defines these two terms more broadly than most people expect, and the exam tests the breadth.

Organization: a person or group of people that has its own functions with responsibilities, authorities, and relationships to achieve its objectives.

The key surprise: even a single person counts as an organization if they have defined responsibilities and authority. A one-person freelancer is an organization. A team within a company is an organization. The whole company is an organization. The exam tests whether you understand this breadth.

Risk: a possible event that could cause harm or loss, or make it more difficult to achieve objectives.

Risk is not always negative in ITIL's broader usage — risk includes uncertainty about outcomes. But on the Foundation exam, the tested definition focuses on the negative: harm, loss, or difficulty achieving objectives.

EXAM TRAP: do not assume 'organization' means 'company.' It can be any group (or individual) with responsibilities and authority.

items.name: Service provision, consumption, and relationship management
items.body:
PURPOSE: these three concepts describe HOW the provider and consumer sides connect — the mechanics of the service interaction.

Service provision: the provider-side activities — managing resources, ensuring access, fulfilling service actions, managing the service level, and continual improvement. This is what the provider DOES.

Service consumption: the consumer-side activities — managing the resources needed to use the service, using the service, and potentially requesting service actions. This is what the consumer DOES.

Service relationship management: the joint activities performed by BOTH provider and consumer to ensure continual value co-creation. This is the shared space where both sides meet.

In your release management world, service provision was your release team providing the deployment capability. Service consumption was the scrum teams using the release process, submitting their intake forms, and attending the war room. Relationship management was the ongoing communication — the feedback loops, the process improvements you made based on team input.

EXAM TRAP: the exam may describe an activity and ask which of these three it belongs to. Provider-only activities = provision. Consumer-only = consumption. Joint activities focused on maintaining the relationship and co-creating value = relationship management.

concepts.note: When a question asks 'what is value,' the answer will contain the word 'perceived.' When it asks about a service, the answer will mention outcomes and the customer not managing costs and risks. When it asks about utility, the answer is about what it DOES (purpose). When it asks about warranty, the answer is about how WELL it performs (use). The wording is that formulaic — learn the keywords and match them.

principles.lead: Seven principles, 6 exam marks, and almost none of them ask you to recite a definition. The exam gives you a scenario — a team doing something right or wrong — and asks which principle it demonstrates. That means you need to read these as BEHAVIORS, not slogans. Each principle has a signature pattern in the scenario: learn the pattern, and the principle names itself. The hardest part is not the principles themselves — it is choosing between two that both seem to fit.
list: Focus on value — but this is almost never the BEST answer when a more specific principle fits
Start where you are — measure what exists before proposing anything new
Progress iteratively with feedback — small chunks, feedback loops, not big-bang
Collaborate and promote visibility — make work visible, involve the right people
Think and work holistically — local optimization can degrade the whole system
Keep it simple and practical — minimum steps, justify every one
Optimize and automate — the ORDER matters: optimize FIRST, then automate

items.name: Focus on value
items.body:
PURPOSE: this principle exists to prevent activity for its own sake. Everything the organization does must link back — directly or indirectly — to value for a stakeholder. If it does not, question whether it should be done at all.

What this means in practice: know who the service consumer is. Understand their actual experience, not what your dashboard says it is. Map every activity back to value — and be willing to stop activities that cannot make the connection.

In your release management world, this is why you tracked release health metrics in Tableau instead of just counting deployments. Counting deployments is activity. Tracking whether those deployments delivered working features to users is value.

EXAM TRAP: 'Focus on value' is almost always too GENERAL to be the best answer. If both 'focus on value' and a more specific principle fit the scenario, pick the specific one. The exam uses 'focus on value' as a plausible-sounding distractor when the scenario is really about visibility, iteration, or simplicity. Only choose it when no other principle fits better.

items.name: Start where you are
items.body:
PURPOSE: this principle exists to prevent the reflexive 'scrap everything and start fresh' that wastes what already works. Before proposing anything new, observe and measure the current state directly — because existing services, people, and processes usually contain reusable value.

Key behaviors:
- Observe and measure directly (do not trust second-hand reports of the current state)
- Identify what can be reused, built on, or improved
- Accept that the current state is imperfect but still holds value
- Use data from the current state to inform the future state

In your release management world, this is exactly what you did every time you pulled the runbook, sat in on release calls, and watched the pipeline before proposing changes. You measured what existed directly before changing anything. When you built the Confluence intake automation, you did not throw out the release process — you automated the intake INTO the existing ServiceNow workflow.

EXAM TRAP: any answer proposing a brand-new solution without assessing the current state first violates this principle. The distractor answer often sounds innovative but skips the 'where are we now' step.

items.name: Progress iteratively with feedback
items.body:
PURPOSE: this principle exists to prevent the 'big-bang' approach where a massive initiative launches after months of planning and delivers feedback only at the end, when the cost of being wrong is highest.

Key behaviors:
- Break work into smaller, manageable, timeboxed sections
- Each section delivers something usable and generates feedback
- Build feedback loops BEFORE, DURING, and AFTER each iteration — not just at the end
- Use that feedback to adjust the plan for the next iteration

In your release management world, this is why your release windows were regular and frequent rather than quarterly big-bang deployments. Each window was a timeboxed delivery that produced real feedback (Dynatrace data, user reports, rollback counts) that informed the next one.

EXAM TRAP: any answer proposing one large initiative without intermediate checkpoints or feedback loops is the distractor for this principle. The exam also tests whether you understand the difference between iterating (doing it in cycles) and just doing it slowly in one pass. The keyword to look for is feedback — if the scenario emphasizes getting feedback at regular intervals, this is the principle.

items.name: Collaborate and promote visibility
items.body:
PURPOSE: this principle exists because poor visibility drives poor decisions and hidden work. When the right people are involved and can see the work and its consequences, better decisions happen naturally.

Key behaviors:
- Include the right stakeholders from the start, not just at review time
- Make work, progress, and blockers visible to everyone who needs to see them
- Share information proactively, do not wait to be asked
- Understand the flow of work and use visibility to find bottlenecks and waste

In your release management world, this is what your war room did — every stakeholder (tech, business, prod support, DevOps) could see the deployment status in real time because you screen-shared each pipeline stage. Publishing a live deployment tracker so every team can see status and blockers is the textbook example of this principle.

EXAM TRAP: when a scenario describes hidden work, a team that does not share status, or a decision made without stakeholder input, this is the principle. Do not confuse it with 'focus on value' — visibility is about WHO SEES the work, not whether the work delivers value.

items.name: Think and work holistically
items.body:
PURPOSE: this principle exists because no service, practice, or component stands alone. Optimizing one part in isolation commonly degrades the system as a whole — the classic local optimization problem.

Key behaviors:
- Consider all four dimensions (organizations/people, information/technology, partners/suppliers, value streams/processes) when making changes
- Recognize that changes in one area ripple through others
- Coordinate across teams and practices, not just within them
- Watch for improvements that help one team but hurt the overall flow

In your release management world, this is why you cared about the blast radius of a monorepo change — a deployment that looked fine from one team's perspective could break three other portals. Your cross-portal conflict checking on the change schedule was holistic thinking in action.

EXAM TRAP: when a scenario describes a local improvement that makes the overall result worse — one team speeds up but the downstream team gets flooded — this is the answer. The keyword pattern is 'improved locally but degraded overall.' 'Focus on value' does not fit here because the local team IS delivering value; the problem is the system-wide impact.

items.name: Keep it simple and practical
items.body:
PURPOSE: this principle exists to prevent over-engineering. Use the minimum number of steps that achieves the objective, and be willing to delete anything that produces no value — including compliance steps that cannot justify their existence.

Key behaviors:
- Start with the simplest approach that works
- Design for the majority of cases; handle exceptions as exceptions
- If a step does not contribute to value, question why it exists
- Do fewer things, but do them well
- Every control must justify itself — including yours

In your release management world, this is why you streamlined the release window end time from past midnight to before 9:40 PM. The extra hours produced no value — they just kept people awake longer. Cutting them was keeping it simple and practical.

EXAM TRAP: any answer that adds complexity, creates elaborate processes for edge cases, or proposes a heavy governance layer for a simple change is violating this principle. The distractor often sounds thorough but is over-engineered. If the scenario asks what to do about a process that has too many steps, this is the answer.

items.name: Optimize and automate
items.body:
PURPOSE: this principle exists to prevent the most common automation mistake — automating a broken process, which just makes the waste run faster.

The order is the entire point: optimize FIRST, then automate.

Optimize: simplify, standardize, and remove waste from the process. Agree the context, assess the current state, agree the future state with simplification, then get stakeholder commitment.
Automate: once the process is clean, automate where it adds value — not everywhere that is technically possible.

In your release management world, this is what happened when you built the Confluence intake automation. You did not automate the messy, manual process as-is — you first defined what a clean intake looked like (required fields, valid fix versions, linked Jira tickets), then automated THAT. Automating the old chaos would have produced automated chaos.

EXAM TRAP: this is one of the most common trap questions. The exam will describe a scenario where someone automates a complex, suboptimal process. The correct answer is 'optimize first.' Any answer that says 'automate it immediately' or reverses the order is wrong. Also tested: technology should not always be relied on without the capability of human intervention.

principles.note: Two habits that pay off on principle questions. First, when 'focus on value' appears alongside a more specific principle, the specific one wins — 'focus on value' is the generic distractor. Second, watch for reversed-order traps on 'optimize and automate' — the order is optimize FIRST, automate SECOND, and the exam tests this directly. Third, 'start where you are' and 'progress iteratively with feedback' overlap in feel; the difference is that 'start where you are' is about ASSESSING the current state, while 'progress iteratively' is about HOW YOU MOVE FORWARD from it.

dimensions.lead: Four lenses that must ALL be considered when designing, managing, or changing any service. Only 2 marks come from here, and they are usually 'name the four dimensions' or 'which dimension does this scenario describe.' The trick is that every scenario touches multiple dimensions — the exam asks which one is PRIMARY. Know the signature pattern for each dimension and you can spot it in the scenario stem.
dimensions.listLabel: The four dimensions of service management
list: Organizations and people — roles, culture, staffing, competencies
Information and technology — what the service knows and what it runs on
Partners and suppliers — every external organization involved
Value streams and processes — how work actually flows from demand to value

items.name: Organizations and people
items.body:
PURPOSE: a service cannot exist without the people who design, deliver, and support it. This dimension ensures you consider not just the org chart but the culture, skills, and authorities that make it work — or prevent it from working.

What it covers: organizational structures, roles and responsibilities, staffing and competencies, and — critically — the culture the organization operates in. ITIL cares whether the culture actually supports the way of working, not just whether the chart looks right.

In your release management world, this is why a reorg that created a new 'DevOps team' but left the old approval chain and risk-averse incentives in place failed to speed up deployments. The structure changed; the culture did not. That disconnect is this dimension.

EXAM TRAP: when a scenario describes a skills gap, a culture mismatch, unclear roles, or an organizational restructuring, this is the dimension. The keyword patterns are 'roles,' 'responsibilities,' 'culture,' 'skills,' and 'competencies.' Do not confuse it with 'partners and suppliers' just because people from outside the org are involved — if the focus is on internal structure and culture, this is the answer.

items.name: Information and technology
items.body:
PURPOSE: every service creates, manages, stores, and depends on information. This dimension ensures you consider both the information itself AND the technology that carries it — including how that information is protected and who can access it.

What it covers: the information a service creates and manages, the technologies required to support it, relationships between components, data security, privacy, and access controls.

The question to ask: 'What does this service know, and what does it run on?'

In your release management world, this is your CMDB — the information about configuration items and their relationships — plus the technology stack (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ServiceNow, Jira) that carried that information. When you assessed blast radius for a monorepo change, you were working in this dimension: what does the service know about its dependencies?

EXAM TRAP: when a scenario mentions data, databases, applications, platforms, or technology choices, this is the dimension. The keyword patterns are 'information,' 'data,' 'technology,' 'systems,' and 'security.' If the focus is on what tool or platform to use, it points here.

items.name: Partners and suppliers
items.body:
PURPOSE: no organization delivers everything alone. This dimension ensures you consider every external organization involved in designing, building, delivering, or supporting the service — and the contracts that govern those relationships.

What it covers: relationships with external organizations, contracts and agreements, sourcing decisions (build vs buy, insource vs outsource), and the level of integration with external partners.

In your release management world, this is your relationship with LaunchDarkly, Dynatrace, and any external vendor whose tool was in the deployment path. When LaunchDarkly was down, your feature flag releases stopped — that dependency was this dimension in action. The contract that defined LaunchDarkly's SLA was also this dimension.

EXAM TRAP: whenever an outside company touches the service, this is the dimension in play. The keyword patterns are 'vendor,' 'supplier,' 'partner,' 'contract,' 'outsource,' and 'third party.' Do not confuse it with 'organizations and people' — that dimension covers internal structure. This one covers external relationships.

items.name: Value streams and processes
items.body:
PURPOSE: this dimension ensures you consider how the actual work flows — the sequence of activities that turns demand into delivered value. Without this dimension, you have people, technology, and partners but no coordinated way for them to produce anything.

Value stream: the end-to-end set of steps an organization takes to create and deliver products and services to a consumer. It maps the path from demand to value.
Process: a set of interrelated activities that transforms inputs into outputs. Processes are the defined steps within the flow.

In your release management world, your swim-lane release workflow (the PowerPoint) IS a value stream map — it shows how a change request flows from intake through approval, build, test, deploy, and validation to reach the user. The individual lanes (scrum team, release management, change management, DevOps) are the processes within that stream.

EXAM TRAP: when a scenario asks 'how does work actually flow here?' or describes a bottleneck in a sequence of activities, this is the dimension. The keyword patterns are 'workflow,' 'steps,' 'sequence,' 'activities,' and 'how value is delivered.' If the question is about the path from request to delivery, it points here.

dimensions.note: All four dimensions are subject to external factors the organization does not control — political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental (PESTLE). If a question asks about something outside the organization's control affecting how it manages services, that is the PESTLE/external factors concept. Remember: the exam question usually touches more than one dimension. Pick the PRIMARY one — the one the scenario stem emphasizes most.

svs.lead: The service value system is the big-picture container that everything else sits inside. Only 1 mark comes from here, usually 'what is the SVS purpose' or 'which of these is a component.' The SVS is not a process, not a maturity model, and not a ranked list. It is the description of how ALL the organization's components and activities work together to create value. Know the five components by name and you own this mark.
svs.listLabel: The five components of the SVS
list: Guiding principles — the seven recommendations that shape everything else
Governance — evaluate, direct, and monitor (the layer that sets policy)
Service value chain — the six-activity operating model (next section)
Practices — 34 sets of organizational resources for performing work
Continual improvement — appears as BOTH a component AND a practice

items.name: What the SVS is for
items.body:
PURPOSE: the SVS exists to prevent the organization from fragmenting into silos that each optimize themselves at the expense of the whole. It describes how ALL components and activities work together as a system to create value.

Definition: it describes how all the components and activities of the organization work together to facilitate value creation through services.

Inputs and outputs: opportunity and demand go in; value comes out. The SVS is the machine that converts what stakeholders need into what stakeholders receive.

In your release management world, the SVS is the entire system — your release process, the change management governance, the tooling, the teams, the improvement cycles — working together to turn a feature request into a production deployment that delivers value to users. No single part does it alone.

EXAM TRAP: if a question calls the SVS a maturity model, a contract, a sequential process, or a ranked list of practices, that answer is wrong. The SVS is a SYSTEM — interconnected components working together. It is also not a lifecycle — that was ITIL v3 (strategy, design, transition, operation, CSI). If those five appear as an option, it is the v3 trap.

items.name: Guiding principles
items.body:
PURPOSE: the principles exist to give the organization stable guidance that applies in EVERY situation, regardless of changes in goals, strategy, structure, or management. They are the constant when everything else is changing.

What they are: seven recommendations that guide the organization in all circumstances. They are covered in full in the Principles section of this app.

Key exam fact: they are recommendations, not mandatory rules and not prescriptive instructions. They help an organization adopt and adapt ITIL guidance to its own context. An organization applies them to its situation — it does not follow them like a checklist.

EXAM TRAP: any answer calling the guiding principles 'mandatory' or 'prescriptive' is wrong. They recommend; they do not require.

items.name: Governance
items.body:
PURPOSE: governance is how the organization is directed and controlled. It sits ABOVE the day-to-day management of services and ensures the organization follows its own policies and stays aligned with its objectives.

The governance loop: evaluate, direct, and monitor.
- Evaluate — assess the current situation and plans
- Direct — set direction and priorities
- Monitor — check that direction is being followed and objectives are being met

In your release management world, governance was the layer above your release process — the policies that said 'no deployments during a freeze,' 'director sign-off required for out-of-window changes,' and 'SOX controls must be met.' You executed the releases; governance set the rules you operated within.

EXAM TRAP: governance is DISTINCT from management. Management runs services day to day. Governance sets the policies and checks that management follows them. If a question asks about who sets the rules (not who follows them), the answer is governance.

items.name: Service value chain
items.body:
PURPOSE: the service value chain is the operating model — six activities that combine in different sequences to convert demand into value. It is the core of the SVS and is covered in detail in the next section.

Key fact: the six activities are NOT sequential. They combine in different orders depending on the value stream. A simple service request might only touch engage and deliver-and-support. A new service might touch all six in multiple passes.

EXAM TRAP: if an answer implies the value chain activities must happen in a fixed order, it is wrong. The value chain is a flexible model, not a linear process.

items.name: Practices
items.body:
PURPOSE: practices are the sets of organizational resources designed for performing work or accomplishing an objective. They are the HOW — the specific capabilities the organization uses to do things.

Key numbers: ITIL 4 defines 34 practices total. The Foundation exam tests 15 of them — 8 at the purpose level only, and 7 in depth. Those 7 account for 17 of 40 marks on the exam.

Each practice draws on all four dimensions (people, technology, partners, processes). Practices contribute to multiple value chain activities — no practice belongs to just one activity.

EXAM TRAP: the ITIL v3 term was 'processes.' ITIL 4 deliberately renamed them 'practices' to emphasize that they include people, technology, and information, not just a sequence of steps. If an answer uses 'process' where ITIL 4 uses 'practice,' watch for the v3 trap.

items.name: Continual improvement
items.body:
PURPOSE: improvement is so important that it appears in the SVS TWICE — once as a component (alongside principles, governance, the value chain, and practices) and once as a practice (one of the 34). This dual appearance is intentional and gets tested.

As an SVS component: continual improvement applies to every other component, every practice, and all four dimensions. It is not something a dedicated team does in a corner — it is everyone's responsibility, embedded in everything the organization does.

Why it is both: the component ensures improvement is woven into the organization's DNA. The practice provides the specific resources, activities, and methods for doing it.

In your release management world, this is why you tracked release metrics in Tableau AND used those metrics to make changes (like cutting the release window end time). The tracking was the practice in action. The organizational expectation that releases should get better every quarter was the component.

EXAM TRAP: the exam will ask 'which SVS component also appears as a practice?' The answer is continual improvement. If it asks 'who is responsible for improvement?' the answer is EVERYONE — not a dedicated team, not management alone.

svs.note: The SVS has exactly five components: guiding principles, governance, service value chain, practices, and continual improvement. If a question offers a sixth or substitutes something else (like 'service lifecycle' or 'maturity framework'), that is the distractor. Remember that continual improvement is BOTH a component and a practice — this exact dual role gets tested.

valuechain.lead: Six activities that combine in different orders to form value streams. Worth 2 marks — usually 'name the six activities' or 'which activity has this purpose.' The critical exam fact is that these activities are NOT sequential and NOT a lifecycle. They combine in whatever order the value stream needs. Each activity has a one-line purpose with keywords that the exam tests directly.
valuechain.listLabel: The six service value chain activities
list: Plan — 'shared understanding of vision, current status, and improvement direction'
Improve — 'continual improvement of products, services, and practices'
Engage — 'understanding stakeholder needs, transparency, and good relationships'
Design and transition — 'meet expectations for quality, cost, and time to market'
Obtain/build — 'service components available when and where needed'
Deliver and support — 'services delivered and supported to agreed specifications'

items.name: Plan
items.body:
PURPOSE: ensures a shared understanding of the vision, current status, and improvement direction — for all four dimensions and all products and services.

The keywords are 'shared understanding' and 'direction.' This is the activity that gets everyone looking at the same horizon. It covers portfolio decisions, resource allocation, and strategic direction — not just project planning.

In your release management world, Plan is what happened when leadership aligned on the release calendar, decided which portals would deploy in which windows, and set the direction for migrating Jenkins builds to pipeline-as-code. The shared understanding of 'here is where we are, here is where we are going' was this activity.

EXAM TRAP: do not confuse Plan with Improve. Plan sets direction; Improve raises the level of what already exists. If the scenario is about establishing a shared vision, it is Plan. If it is about making current practices better, it is Improve.

items.name: Improve
items.body:
PURPOSE: ensures continual improvement of products, services, and practices across ALL value chain activities and all four dimensions.

The keyword is 'improvement.' This activity applies everywhere — it is not limited to one practice or one team. Any effort to make something better than it currently is falls here.

In your release management world, Improve is what you did when you analyzed release health data in Tableau, identified that late-night deployments correlated with higher rollback rates, and changed the window end time. You measured, identified the problem, and made it better. That is Improve.

EXAM TRAP: Improve is the value chain activity. 'Continual improvement' is both a practice AND an SVS component. The exam can ask about any of the three — read the question stem carefully to know which level it is asking about. If it asks 'which value chain activity,' the answer is Improve. If it asks 'which practice,' the answer is continual improvement.

items.name: Engage
items.body:
PURPOSE: provides a good understanding of stakeholder needs, transparency, and continual engagement and good relationships with all stakeholders.

The keyword is 'stakeholder.' This is the activity that faces OUTWARD — customers, users, suppliers, partners, anyone who has a stake in the service. It covers understanding needs, managing expectations, and maintaining the relationship.

In your release management world, Engage is the intake process where scrum teams submitted their release requests, the war room where stakeholders were present for every deployment, and the release notes you published to keep business users informed. Every interaction where you understood what they needed or kept them informed was this activity.

EXAM TRAP: Engage is about the relationship with stakeholders. 'Deliver and support' is about fulfilling the service. If the scenario is about understanding what the stakeholder wants or maintaining the relationship, it is Engage. If the scenario is about actually providing the service, it is Deliver and support.

items.name: Design and transition
items.body:
PURPOSE: ensures products and services continually meet stakeholder expectations for quality, cost, and time to market.

All three keywords are named in the purpose. A question that mentions any of them — especially time to market — is pointing at this activity. It covers the design of new services, the transition of changes into production, and the ongoing assurance that what is delivered meets expectations.

In your release management world, Design and transition is what happened when a new portal was being onboarded to the release process. The team designed how it would fit into the existing deployment pipeline, defined the intake requirements, and transitioned it into the regular release cadence. The goal was meeting quality, cost, and time expectations.

EXAM TRAP: if the scenario mentions 'time to market,' this is almost certainly the answer. No other value chain activity includes that phrase in its purpose.

items.name: Obtain/build
items.body:
PURPOSE: ensures service components are available when and where they are needed, and that they meet agreed specifications.

The keywords are 'components,' 'available,' and 'specifications.' This activity covers both building in-house and procuring from outside — it does not care whether you made it or bought it, only that the component is there when needed and meets the agreed specs.

In your release management world, Obtain/build is what happened when the DevOps team built a new deployment pipeline in GitHub Actions, or when the organization procured LaunchDarkly for feature flag management. In both cases, a service component was made available to meet agreed requirements.

EXAM TRAP: the '/' in 'Obtain/build' is deliberate — it covers BOTH procurement (obtain) and development (build). Do not assume it is only about building software. If the scenario describes getting a component ready — whether by building it internally or buying it from a vendor — this is the activity.

items.name: Deliver and support
items.body:
PURPOSE: ensures services are delivered and supported according to agreed specifications and stakeholder expectations.

The keywords are 'delivered' and 'supported.' This is where the service desk, incident management, and service request management live day to day. It is the activity that keeps the lights on and the users served.

In your release management world, Deliver and support is the production environment running, the service desk fielding calls when something breaks, and your team responding to incidents during and after the release window. The war room during a deployment was this activity in action — delivering the release and supporting it through validation.

EXAM TRAP: do not confuse Deliver and support with Engage. Engage is about understanding stakeholder needs and maintaining relationships. Deliver and support is about actually providing the service and handling issues. If the scenario describes fulfilling service requests or resolving incidents, it is Deliver and support.

valuechain.note: The value chain replaced the ITIL v3 lifecycle (strategy, design, transition, operation, CSI). If those five appear as an option, that is the trap answer pointing at the old version. The six activities are NOT sequential — they combine in different orders depending on the value stream. A simple request might touch only Engage and Deliver and support. A new service might loop through all six activities multiple times. If a question implies a fixed sequence, that answer is wrong.

practices15.lead: A practice is a set of organizational resources designed for performing work. ITIL 4 has 34 practices; Foundation tests 15 of them. Seven of those 15 need real depth and get their own section — this brief covers the other 8, where knowing the one-line purpose is genuinely all you need. But that purpose must be EXACT: the exam tests specific keywords in each purpose statement. This section also includes 7 term definitions (IT asset, event, CI, change, incident, problem, known error) worth 2 marks.
practices15.listLabel: The 15 practices you must know the purpose of
list: Information security management — protect information (CIA + authentication + non-repudiation)
Relationship management — strategic and tactical stakeholder links (not contracts)
Supplier management — contracts and supplier performance (not relationships)
IT asset management — lifecycle, financially valuable, NOT the same as config management
Monitoring and event management — detect and report state changes (does NOT restore)
Release management — make services and features available for use (YOUR lane)
Service configuration management — relationships and dependencies between CIs
Deployment management — physically move components to live environments
— the seven below get their own section —
Continual improvement
Change enablement
Incident management
Problem management
Service request management
Service desk
Service level management

items.name: Information security management
items.body:
PURPOSE: protect the information the organization needs to conduct its business. This means managing confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) — plus authentication and non-repudiation.

What each term means:
- Confidentiality — only authorized people see it
- Integrity — it has not been tampered with
- Availability — it is there when you need it
- Authentication — you are who you claim to be
- Non-repudiation — you cannot deny you did what you did

In your release management world, this is the SOX compliance lane — the segregation-of-duties controls you enforced, the audit trails in ServiceNow, and the requirement that the person who built the code was not the person who deployed it to production. All information security management.

EXAM TRAP: this practice is about protecting information, not about running access requests — access requests are service requests. If the scenario asks about granting a user access to a system, that is service request management. If it asks about the POLICY governing who should have access, that is information security management.

items.name: Relationship management
items.body:
PURPOSE: establish and nurture the links between the organization and its stakeholders at strategic and tactical levels.

This is the relationship side — understanding stakeholder needs, maintaining trust, ensuring stakeholders feel heard. It is NOT about contracts or vendor performance — that is supplier management.

The distinction: relationship management is about the HUMAN CONNECTION. Supplier management is about the COMMERCIAL AGREEMENT. A healthy vendor relationship needs both practices, but they are separate.

In your release management world, this is the work you did building trust with 60+ scrum teams — understanding their release needs, communicating the deployment calendar, resolving conflicts when two teams wanted the same window. That was relationship management. The contract with LaunchDarkly or Dynatrace was supplier management.

EXAM TRAP: the exam likes to swap these two. If the scenario describes nurturing stakeholder trust and understanding needs, it is relationship management. If it describes managing contracts and ensuring vendor performance, it is supplier management.

items.name: Supplier management
items.body:
PURPOSE: ensure the organization's suppliers and their performance are managed appropriately to support the seamless provision of quality products and services.

The keywords are 'suppliers' and 'performance.' This covers contracts, SLAs with vendors, performance tracking, and the sourcing relationship — buy vs build decisions, multi-vendor coordination, and contract governance.

In your release management world, this is the contractual relationship with your external tooling vendors — the SLA that said Dynatrace would be available 99.9% of the time, the performance reviews of LaunchDarkly's reliability. When a vendor's tool was in your deployment path, supplier management governed that dependency.

EXAM TRAP: supplier management is about contracts and commercial performance. Relationship management is about trust and stakeholder engagement. A scenario about a vendor underperforming against their SLA is supplier management. A scenario about building a better working relationship with that same vendor is relationship management.

items.name: IT asset management
items.body:
PURPOSE: plan and manage the full lifecycle of all IT assets to maximize value, control costs, manage risks, and support decisions about purchase, reuse, and retirement.

IT asset definition: any financially valuable component that can contribute to the delivery of an IT product or service.

The keyword is 'financially valuable' — this is a tested definition. Assets have cost, ownership, and a lifecycle (acquire, use, maintain, retire). Configuration items have relationships and dependencies. A server is both an asset (it cost money, it depreciates) and a CI (it connects to other components).

The distinction from service configuration management:
- Asset management cares about ownership, cost, and lifecycle
- Configuration management cares about relationships, dependencies, and how things are wired together
- Many items are BOTH an asset AND a CI

EXAM TRAP: this distinction gets tested directly. If the question is about 'how much did it cost and when does the license expire,' that is asset management. If the question is about 'what else breaks if this goes down,' that is configuration management.

items.name: Monitoring and event management
items.body:
PURPOSE: systematically observe services and service components, and record and report selected changes of state identified as events.

Event definition: any change of state that has significance for the management of a service or other configuration item. Events are typically recognized through notifications created by a service, CI, or monitoring tool.

Three event types:
- Informational — no action needed, recorded for reference (a backup completed successfully)
- Warning — something is approaching a threshold, action may be needed soon (disk usage at 85%)
- Exception — something has breached a threshold or failed, action IS needed (service down)

In your release management world, this is Dynatrace watching the production environment after every deployment. 'Dynatrace clear' was an informational event confirming no exceptions. A spike in error rates after a deploy was an exception event that triggered your rollback decision.

EXAM TRAP: monitoring and event management detects — it does NOT restore. Restoring service is incident management. If the scenario asks about detecting a problem, this practice. If it asks about fixing it, that is incident management.

items.name: Release management
items.body:
PURPOSE: make new and changed services and features available for use.

'Available for use' is the entire definition and the tested keyword. This practice is about the decision and action of making something available to users — not about moving code to servers (that is deployment management).

This is your lane. ITIL 4 splits release from deployment in a way most enterprises do not, and the distinction is the most frequently tested pair in this section.

The release vs deployment distinction:
- Deployment = moving code to the production environment
- Release = making it available to users

A feature pushed to production behind a flag that is switched off has been deployed but not released. When you flip the flag on, the feature is released with no new deployment.

In your release management world, this is exactly what happened with LaunchDarkly. The deploy was the pipeline run. The release was the flag flip that made the feature visible to users.

EXAM TRAP: if the exam describes code in production that users cannot see yet, the state is 'deployed but not released.' If it describes users gaining access to a new feature, the practice is release management.

items.name: Deployment management
items.body:
PURPOSE: move new or changed hardware, software, documentation, processes, or any other component to live environments. It may also deploy to staging or test environments.

The keyword is 'move.' This is the physical (or virtual) act of putting components where they need to be. It does not care whether users can see the result — that is release management's concern.

In your release management world, this is the pipeline run itself — triggering the build, test, and deploy stages in GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or uDeploy. When you pressed run and watched each stage on the screen share, you were doing deployment management. When you later confirmed the feature was available to users, that was release management.

Deployment approaches (for recognition):
- Phased — deploy to a subset of environments first, then expand
- Continuous delivery — automated pipeline deploys frequently
- Big bang — deploy everything at once
- Pull — the target environment pulls the update when ready

EXAM TRAP: deployment works closely with release management and change enablement, but they are three separate practices with three separate purposes. Deploy = move it. Release = make it available. Change enablement = authorize it.

items.name: Service configuration management
items.body:
PURPOSE: ensure that accurate and reliable information about the configuration of services, and the CIs that support them, is available when and where it is needed. This includes information about how CIs are configured and how they relate to each other.

Configuration item (CI) definition: any component that needs to be managed in order to deliver an IT service. CIs typically include hardware, software, networks, buildings, people, suppliers, and documentation.

The keyword is 'relationships.' This practice cares about what is connected to what — the dependencies between components. If Server A goes down, what else is affected? That is configuration management thinking.

In your release management world, this is your monorepo blast-radius assessment. When you checked which portals would be affected by a shared-library change, you were using configuration management thinking — tracing the relationships between CIs to understand the impact. Your CI identification on intake (the approximately 30 CMDB CIs in the AWS migration) was this practice in action.

EXAM TRAP: configuration management is about relationships and dependencies. Asset management is about cost and lifecycle. A CI is any component that needs managing. An IT asset is any financially valuable component. Many items are both — but the questions ask about the PRACTICE, not the item.

practices15.note: Release vs deployment is the pair to burn in — it is your subject and the most tested distinction in this section. A feature pushed to production behind a flag that is off has been DEPLOYED but not RELEASED. Flip it: a feature can be released to users the instant a flag flips, with no deployment happening that day. In ITIL terms, what you did with LaunchDarkly was release management, and triggering the pipeline was deployment management. Also: the 7 defined terms (IT asset, event, CI, change, incident, problem, known error) are worth 2 marks. Know the exact definitions.

practices7.lead: Seventeen of the 40 exam questions come from this section — more than everything else combined. These seven practices must be UNDERSTOOD, not just recalled: the questions describe a situation and ask which practice owns it, or what should happen next. The single most important skill is sorting a scenario into the right bucket: is it an incident, a problem, a known error, a service request, an event, or a change? Get the bucket right and the answer usually follows.
practices7.listLabel: The seven practices covered in detail
list: Continual improvement — everyone's responsibility, seven-step model, baseline is the step that gets skipped
Change enablement — MAXIMIZE successful changes (not restrict them), three types, standard is pre-authorized
Incident management — restore service ASAP, close with a workaround if needed, root cause is NOT the goal
Problem management — three phases (identification, control, error control), known error = analyzed but not resolved
Service request management — pre-defined, nothing is broken, standardize and automate
Service desk — single point of contact, four models, the empathetic front door
Service level management — business-based targets, watermelon effect, three valid data sources

items.name: Continual improvement
items.body:
PURPOSE: align the organization's practices and services with changing business needs through ongoing identification and improvement of every element of management of services and products. This practice is the engine that keeps everything else getting better.

Key exam facts:
- Improvement is everyone's responsibility — not just a dedicated team, though at least a small team should lead it
- It is integral to every other practice — not a separate, siloed activity
- Suppliers should be included in improvement activities
- Pick a few key improvement methods that suit the organization — do not adopt every method available, and do not switch methods constantly
- Accurate data is the foundation of fact-based decisions

The continual improvement model — seven steps:
1. What is the vision?
2. Where are we now?
3. Where do we want to be?
4. How do we get there?
5. Take action
6. Did we get there?
7. How do we keep the momentum going?

In your release management world, this is what you did with the Tableau release health dashboard — measured where you were, identified problems, made changes, and measured again. The release window time cut (past midnight to before 9:40 PM) was this model in action.

EXAM TRAP: the step organizations skip most is step 2 — 'Where are we now?' Without a baseline, you can never answer 'Did we get there?' in step 6. Any answer that jumps to solutions without establishing the current state is skipping the baseline.

items.name: Change enablement
items.body:
PURPOSE: maximize the number of successful service and product changes by ensuring risks are properly assessed, authorizing changes to proceed, and managing the change schedule.

Read that emphasis again: MAXIMIZE successful changes. This practice exists to get changes through safely, not to block them. Any answer framing change enablement as restriction or gatekeeping is wrong.

Three change types (the exam tests these constantly):
- Standard: low-risk, pre-authorized, well-understood, fully documented. Needs NO per-instance approval — it was risk-assessed and authorized when its procedure was created. Often initiated as a service request.
- Normal: must be scheduled, assessed, and authorized following a defined process. Change models set the roles for assessment and authorization.
- Emergency: must be implemented as soon as possible (incident, security patch). Assessment and authorization are expedited but should follow the same rigor as normal changes 'as far as possible.' Not typically on the change schedule.

Change authority: the person or group who authorizes a change. The correct authority must be assigned to each type — a single change authority for everything is explicitly marked wrong in the official papers.

Change schedule: used BEFORE deployment to plan, communicate, avoid conflicts, and assign resources. Used AFTER deployment to inform incident management, problem management, and improvement planning.

In your release management world, this is your entire go/no-go process. Standard changes were your well-understood, repeatable deployments. Normal changes went through your full intake and approval cycle. Emergency changes were out-of-window pushes with director sign-off.

EXAM TRAP: 'routine' is NOT a change type in ITIL 4. The three types are standard, normal, and emergency. 'Routine' is a trap answer that appears on multiple practice exams. Also: emergency changes are NOT exempt from assessment — they get the same rigor, just faster.

items.name: Incident management
items.body:
PURPOSE: minimize the negative impact of incidents by restoring normal service operation as quickly as possible.

Incident definition: an unplanned interruption to a service, or a reduction in the quality of a service.

Speed of restoration is THE objective. Finding the root cause is explicitly NOT the goal of incident management — that belongs to problem management. An incident closes when service is restored, even if the restoration is a workaround and the underlying fault is still there.

Key exam facts:
- Every incident is logged and managed to agreed resolution times
- Prioritized by agreed classification — highest business impact first
- Routing is typically by incident category
- Anyone can report an incident — users, technical staff, or monitoring tools
- Major incidents often require a temporary team to be formed
- Incident management should NOT include detailed diagnosis procedures — those belong in knowledge articles or with specialist teams
- Tools can auto-match incidents to other incidents, problems, or known errors

In your release management world, this is your war room. When a deployment broke something, the goal was restore service NOW — not figure out why it broke (that is the post-mortem, which is problem management). Your 15-minute rollback SLA was incident management: minimize impact, restore service, figure out the cause later.

EXAM TRAP: if a scenario describes someone investigating root cause during an active outage instead of restoring service, that is the wrong approach. Restore first, investigate later. Also: an incident closed with a workaround is still properly closed — the underlying problem becomes a problem record.

items.name: Problem management
items.body:
PURPOSE: reduce the likelihood and impact of incidents by identifying actual and potential causes of incidents, and managing workarounds and known errors.

Problem definition: a cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents.
Known error definition: a problem that has been analysed but not yet resolved.

Three phases:
1. Problem identification — spotting patterns: trend analysis of incident records, detecting duplicate and recurring incidents, and analyzing information from other practices
2. Problem control — analyzing the problem to understand the root cause
3. Error control — managing the known error once the cause is understood but a fix is not yet in place; may include raising a change request if justified by cost, risk, and benefit

Key exam facts:
- Problems are prioritized by risk — NOT every problem needs analysis
- Workarounds are documented in problem records and one can become permanent if a full fix is not cost-effective
- Error control may result in a change request, but only if justified
- Solutions can be placed on a continual improvement register

In your release management world, this is the next-day post-mortem. After the incident was resolved (service restored), you investigated WHY it happened — that shift from 'fix it now' to 'understand why' is the handoff from incident management to problem management.

EXAM TRAP: incident vs problem is the most heavily tested distinction in all of ITIL 4 Foundation. Incident = restore service NOW. Problem = understand WHY and prevent recurrence. Known error = we understand it but have not fixed it yet. A workaround lives in the problem record, not the incident record.

items.name: Service request management
items.body:
PURPOSE: support the agreed quality of a service by handling all pre-defined, user-initiated service requests in an effective and user-friendly manner.

The keywords are 'pre-defined' and 'nothing is broken.' Service requests are normal parts of service delivery that are already agreed and already authorized. There is no incident, no investigation, no approval process needed — the request type was approved when it was created.

Key exam facts:
- Requests should be standardized and automated wherever possible
- They are usually fulfilled as standard changes
- They are user-initiated (the user asks for something, not something breaking)
- Clear expectations for fulfilment times must be set and communicated
- Policies governing what can be requested, who can request it, and the approval workflow should be established up front

In your release management world, the Confluence intake form your scrum teams filled out was a service request — a pre-defined, standardized way to request a release slot. Nobody was reporting a problem; they were asking for something they were entitled to as part of normal service delivery.

EXAM TRAP: the distinction from incidents is critical. Incident = something is broken or degraded. Service request = nothing is broken, the user wants something normal (access, information, a standard change). If the scenario describes a user asking for something pre-defined and routine, it is a service request, not an incident.

items.name: Service desk
items.body:
PURPOSE: capture demand for incident resolution and service requests. It is the single point of contact between the service provider and all of its users — the entry point, not necessarily the team that fixes the problem.

Key exam facts:
- Issues, queries, and requests are acknowledged, classified, owned, and actioned
- The service desk needs practical understanding of the wider organization, business processes, and users
- It does not need to be highly technical — its value is often as the empathetic front door
- Escalation to specialist teams will always be needed — this is normal, not a failure
- Automation and self-service are increasingly shifting how it operates

Four structural models:
- Local — co-located with users, same physical location
- Centralized — fewer locations serving many users remotely
- Virtual — distributed staff using technology to appear as one desk
- Follow-the-sun — desks in multiple time zones providing 24-hour coverage

In your release management world, the service desk was the first point of contact when users reported a problem after a deployment. They logged the incident, classified it, and either resolved it or escalated it to your war room. They were the front door; you were the specialist team behind it.

EXAM TRAP: 'outsourced' is NOT a service desk model. The four models are local, centralized, virtual, and follow-the-sun. 'Outsourced' describes WHO runs the desk, not HOW it is structured — it can apply to any of the four models.

items.name: Service level management
items.body:
PURPOSE: set clear business-based targets for service performance, so that the delivery of services can be properly assessed, monitored, and managed against those targets.

The keyword is 'business-based.' Targets must relate to outcomes that matter to the business, not just technical metrics. This is the most heavily emphasized point in the practice.

The watermelon effect: SLA dashboards are all green on the outside (every technical metric met), but the actual user experience is red on the inside (users are unhappy, business outcomes are not being achieved). This happens when SLAs are built on component metrics (uptime, response time) instead of business outcomes (can the user complete their transaction?).

Three valid SLA data sources:
1. Customer feedback — surveys, meetings, qualitative input
2. Business-related metrics — metrics tied to business outcomes (transaction completion, conversion rates)
3. Operational metrics — system performance data (availability, response time)

All three together give a balanced view. Using only operational metrics is how the watermelon effect starts.

In your release management world, this is why you tracked release health in Tableau instead of just reporting 'pipeline ran successfully.' The pipeline metric was operational (it ran). The business metric was whether the feature actually worked for users. If you only reported the pipeline metric, you would have had a watermelon — green pipeline, red user experience.

EXAM TRAP: competitor benchmarks are NOT a valid SLA data source. The three valid sources are customer feedback, business metrics, and operational metrics. If 'competitor analysis' or 'industry benchmarks' appears as an option for how to set SLA targets, it is the distractor. Also: a single metric like 'percentage availability' should not stand for the whole service — targets need balanced bundles of metrics.

practices7.note: The sorting question that decides most of these 17 marks: incident (restore it now) vs problem (understand why, prevent recurrence) vs known error (understood, not fixed yet) vs event (a change of state, often harmless) vs service request (nothing is broken, user wants something normal). Get the bucket right and the answer follows. TRAP: 'routine' is NOT a change type — the three types are standard, normal, and emergency. TRAP: 'outsourced' is NOT a service desk model — the four models are local, centralized, virtual, and follow-the-sun. TRAP: change enablement exists to MAXIMIZE successful changes, not to restrict them. TRAP: incident management closes when service is restored, even with a workaround — root cause investigation is problem management.
terms: routine (NOT a change type — exam trap)
